**Visual Analysis:**

- **Plant/part affected**: Wheat leaves at the rosette/early stem stage, viewed from above
- **Key features on the central prominent leaf**:
  - Pale yellow to cream-white **stripes running parallel to leaf veins** (longitudinally along the leaf)
  - Stripes appear somewhat diffuse/broad rather than discrete pustule rows
  - Small yellowish spots also visible on surrounding leaves
  - Overall plant still green; not severely necrotic
- **Pattern**: The striping is clearly aligned with venation, which is the hallmark of stripe rust (*Puccinia striiformis*)

**Differential reasoning:**

| Class | Evidence For | Evidence Against |
|---|---|---|
| **Stripe Rust** | Classic yellow stripes parallel to veins on wheat; small pustule-like dots visible | Color is paler/cream rather than bright orange-yellow of mature pustules |
| Cephalosporium Stripe | Pale cream-yellow stripes matching color | Usually more white/bleached, associated with vascular wilting |
| Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus | Causes yellowing | More uniform tip yellowing, not stripe-patterned |
| Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus | Yellow streaking | Mosaic/mottled, not clean parallel stripes |

The clean linear striping aligned with leaf venation is the textbook signature of **Stripe Rust** in early to mid-stage infection, before pustules fully mature to orange. The pale yellow color is consistent with early-stage urediniospore development.

The linear, vein-parallel stripe pattern rules out mosaic viruses (which cause irregular mottling) and BYDV (which causes tip yellowing), and is more consistent with stripe rust than Cephalosporium stripe (which typically causes more bleached, systemic wilting)."}
